title: Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures
subject: Science
chapter: 8. Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures
description: Mixtures (uniform and non-uniform, alloys, air), pure substances, elements, compounds, the electrolysis of water, the iron–sulfur experiment, minerals and the chapter's exercises.

questions.question: According to the chapter, what is a mixture?
options: Two or more substances mixed together, each keeping its own properties
Two or more elements joined chemically in a fixed ratio of atoms
A single kind of matter made of only one type of particle throughout
A substance that cannot be broken into anything simpler by any method
questions.explanation: A mixture forms when two or more substances are mixed and each substance retains its properties; the components do not react chemically. The other options describe a compound, a pure substance and an element.

questions.question: The individual substances that make up a mixture are called its…
options: chemical products
components
molecules
constituent atoms
questions.explanation: The chapter defines the individual substances making up a mixture as its components. Atoms and molecules are particles of a substance, and 'products' are what a chemical reaction makes.

questions.question: A student mixes iron filings with sand and finds that a magnet still pulls out the iron. What does this show about the mixture?
options: The mixture has become a pure substance after mixing
The components have combined in a fixed ratio by mass
Each component keeps its own properties in the mixture
The iron and sand have reacted to form a new substance
questions.explanation: In a mixture the components retain their individual properties and do not react chemically, so iron is still magnetic and can be pulled out. A new substance, a fixed ratio or purity would indicate a compound, not a mixture.

questions.question: A sprout salad of green gram, chickpeas, onion and tomato is a non-uniform mixture because…
options: its components react chemically with one another
its components are evenly spread and cannot be told apart
it contains both solids and liquids mixed together
its components can be seen separately with the naked eye
questions.explanation: Mixtures whose different components are visible with the naked eye or a magnifying device are non-uniform. Evenly distributed, indistinguishable components would make it uniform; components of a mixture never react chemically.

questions.question: Why is a solution of sugar in water called a uniform mixture?
options: Sugar and water particles cannot be seen separately even with a microscope
Sugar and water combine chemically to form a sweet new compound
Sugar crystals can be seen floating evenly through the water
The sugar settles at the bottom in an even layer over time
questions.explanation: In a uniform mixture the components are evenly distributed and cannot be distinguished, even under a microscope. Sugar does not react chemically with water, and visible crystals or a settled layer would make the mixture non-uniform.

questions.question: Which statement about mixtures is NOT correct?
options: Sugar dissolved in water, soups and lemonade are all mixtures
The components of a mixture lose their original properties
The components of a mixture do not react chemically with each other
Some mixtures have components visible with a magnifying device
questions.explanation: In a mixture each substance retains its properties — that is the defining feature. The other three statements are directly stated in the chapter.

questions.question: In common usage, poha is a mixture of ingredients that are themselves mixtures. In science, however, the components of a mixture must be…
options: liquids or gases only
elements, never compounds
pure substances only
visible to the naked eye
questions.explanation: The chapter states that in science all the components of a mixture must be pure substances (elements or compounds). Components need not be visible, can be in any state, and compounds like sugar or salt are allowed.

questions.question: Sugar dissolved in water is an example of a mixture.
questions.explanation: The chapter lists sugar dissolved in water, soups and lemonade as everyday mixtures; sugar and water keep their own properties.

questions.question: The components of a uniform mixture can be seen separately with the help of a microscope.
questions.explanation: In a uniform mixture the components cannot be seen separately even with a microscope; it is the non-uniform mixtures whose components are visible with the eye or a magnifying device.

questions.question: Select the mixtures described in the chapter as non-uniform (components visible).
options: Sprout salad
Poha
Sugar dissolved in water
Air
questions.explanation: Sprout salad and poha have components you can see, so they are non-uniform. Sugar solution and air are uniform mixtures whose components cannot be distinguished.

questions.question: In ancient Indian texts, 'Mishraloha' referred to…
options: a compound of a metal and a non-metal formed by heating them strongly together
a pure metal purified repeatedly until no other substance remained in it
a mineral containing a single metal in its natural, uncombined state
a mixture of two or more metals with properties distinct from its constituent metals
questions.explanation: Mishraloha was the name given to a mixture of two or more metals (an alloy) whose properties were distinct from those of its constituent metals.

questions.question: Bronze, known as Kamsya in ancient texts, is an alloy of…
options: copper (4 parts) and tin (1 part)
copper (4 parts) and zinc (1 part)
iron (4 parts) and nickel (1 part)
tin (4 parts) and copper (1 part)
questions.explanation: Kamsya (bronze) is described as copper (Tamra, 4 parts) and tin (Vanga, 1 part). Copper and zinc make brass; iron and nickel are in stainless steel; the copper-to-tin ratio is 4:1, not reversed.

questions.question: According to the texts cited in the chapter, Kamsya (bronze) was used medicinally to…
options: strengthen bones and heal fractures
improve digestion and boost immunity
cure fevers and reduce body heat
purify water and remove dust from it
questions.explanation: The chapter states that bronze (Kamsya) was used to improve digestion and boost immunity. The other uses are not mentioned.

questions.question: Stainless steel is a uniform mixture containing…
options: iron, copper, tin and a small amount of sulfur
aluminium, iron, chromium and a little silicon
iron, nickel, chromium and a small amount of carbon
copper, zinc, nickel and a small amount of carbon
questions.explanation: Stainless steel contains iron, nickel, chromium and a small amount of carbon mixed so uniformly that it looks the same throughout. Copper–zinc is brass and copper–tin is bronze.

questions.question: Brass is an alloy made of…
options: copper and tin
iron and chromium
zinc and tin
copper and zinc
questions.explanation: Brass is a mixture of copper and zinc; bronze is copper and tin; iron and chromium are found in stainless steel.

questions.question: Why are alloys such as stainless steel classified as uniform mixtures?
options: The metals are mixed so evenly that no individual substance can be seen anywhere
The metals react chemically to form a new compound with a fixed ratio
The metals keep separate layers that can be seen with a magnifying glass
Each metal can be seen as separate grains when the alloy is cut open
questions.explanation: In an alloy the metals are mixed so uniformly that the whole appears the same throughout and individual substances cannot be seen — the definition of a uniform mixture. Alloys are not compounds, and visible layers or grains would make them non-uniform.

questions.question: Which statement about alloys is NOT correct?
options: Alloys are mixtures in which individual metals cannot be seen
Brass is a compound of copper and zinc formed in a fixed ratio
Bronze is an alloy made from copper and tin
Stainless steel is a mixture and is stronger than pure iron
questions.explanation: Brass is an alloy, which is a uniform mixture of copper and zinc — not a compound. The other three statements agree with the chapter.

questions.question: Bronze is a mixture of copper and zinc.
questions.explanation: Bronze is copper and tin; copper and zinc make brass.

questions.question: Stainless steel contains a small amount of carbon, a non-metal.
questions.explanation: Stainless steel contains iron, nickel, chromium and a small amount of carbon; carbon is listed as a non-metal in the chapter.

questions.question: Which of the following are alloys?
options: Stainless steel
Bronze
Iron sulfide
Quartz
questions.explanation: Stainless steel and bronze are alloys (uniform mixtures of metals). Iron sulfide is a compound, and quartz is a mineral.

questions.question: Air is a uniform mixture of mainly…
options: oxygen, carbon dioxide, ozone, sulfur dioxide and dust
nitrogen, hydrogen, argon, carbon monoxide and dust
nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour
nitrogen, oxygen, hydrogen, helium and water vapour
questions.explanation: The chapter lists air as a uniform mixture mainly of nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour. Hydrogen and helium are not listed; ozone, SO2, CO and dust are pollutants.

questions.question: About what percentage of air is nitrogen?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen constitutes about 78% of air. 21% is the approximate share of oxygen (from earlier grades), and the other values are not mentioned.

questions.question: Which gas in air does NOT take part in combustion, according to the chapter?
options: Nitrogen
Oxygen
Hydrogen
Water vapour
questions.explanation: Nitrogen, about 78% of air, does not take part in combustion. Oxygen helps combustion and hydrogen is itself a fuel.

questions.question: Which gas in air is required by most living beings and also helps in combustion?
options: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Nitrogen
Argon
questions.explanation: Oxygen is required by most living beings to stay alive and helps in combustion; nitrogen does not take part in combustion.

questions.question: Tiny water droplets form when warm air touches a cool surface. What does this show?
options: Cool surfaces release water that was stored inside them
Carbon dioxide in the air dissolves to form liquid droplets
Air contains water vapour that condenses into liquid water
Air contains oxygen that turns into water on cooling
questions.explanation: When warm air touches a cool surface, the water vapour in the air turns into liquid water, forming tiny droplets — evidence that air has water vapour.

questions.question: A candle burns in a sealed jar of air and then goes out. Based on the chapter, which gas was used up and which gas remained unchanged?
options: Nitrogen was used up; oxygen remained unchanged
Carbon dioxide was used up; argon remained unchanged
Water vapour was used up; oxygen remained unchanged
Oxygen was used up; nitrogen remained unchanged
questions.explanation: Oxygen helps combustion, so it is consumed; nitrogen (about 78% of air) does not take part in combustion and remains. Carbon dioxide is produced, not consumed.

questions.question: Nitrogen makes up about 21% of the air.
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is about 78% of air; 21% is roughly the share of oxygen.

questions.question: Air is classified in Table 8.1 as a uniform gas-and-gas mixture.
questions.explanation: Table 8.1 lists air as a gas and gas mixture and marks it uniform.

questions.question: Which of these are named in the chapter as components of air (not pollutants)?
options: Argon
Water vapour
Sulfur dioxide
Carbon monoxide
questions.explanation: Argon and water vapour are listed among the main components of air. Sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide are named as air pollutants.

questions.topic: Testing Air: Lime Water and Dust
questions.question: In Activity 8.1, what happens when calcium oxide (quick lime) is added to water?
options: It reacts vigorously to form calcium hydroxide and releases heat
It dissolves quietly to form a milky calcium carbonate solution
It floats on the water without reacting and absorbs heat
It releases carbon dioxide bubbles and cools the water down
questions.explanation: Calcium oxide reacts vigorously with water to form calcium hydroxide and releases heat, which is why the step must be done carefully.

questions.topic: Testing Air: Lime Water and Dust
questions.question: Lime water is a solution of…
options: carbon dioxide
calcium hydroxide
calcium oxide
calcium carbonate
questions.explanation: Stirring calcium oxide in water gives a solution of calcium hydroxide, which is called lime water. Calcium carbonate is the insoluble product that makes it milky.

questions.topic: Testing Air: Lime Water and Dust
questions.question: Why does lime water turn milky in air?
options: Dust particles from the air settle into the solution and cloud it
Water vapour from the air condenses and dilutes the clear solution
Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate
Oxygen reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium oxide
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide in the air reacts with calcium hydroxide to form calcium carbonate (tiny insoluble white particles) and water, which makes the solution milky.

questions.topic: Testing Air: Lime Water and Dust
questions.question: Complete the word equation: Calcium hydroxide + Carbon dioxide → ______ + Water
options: Calcium oxide
Calcium chloride
Carbon monoxide
Calcium carbonate
questions.explanation: The reaction is Calcium hydroxide + Carbon dioxide → Calcium carbonate + Water. Calcium carbonate is the insoluble white solid.

questions.topic: Testing Air: Lime Water and Dust
questions.question: In Activity 8.1 the filtered lime water was left in a petri dish for a few hours and turned milky. What does this demonstrate?
options: Carbon dioxide is present in the air
Oxygen is present in the air
Water vapour is present in the air
Dust particles are present in the air
questions.explanation: Lime water turns milky only when carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide, so milkiness on exposure to air demonstrates the presence of carbon dioxide in air.

questions.topic: Testing Air: Lime Water and Dust
questions.question: Predict: If freshly filtered lime water is sealed immediately in an airtight, air-free container, what would most likely be observed after a few hours?
options: It turns yellow because the calcium oxide settles at the bottom
It stays colourless because no carbon dioxide reaches it
It turns milky because calcium hydroxide slowly decomposes
It turns milky because water vapour cannot escape from it
questions.explanation: Milkiness requires carbon dioxide from the air reacting with calcium hydroxide. With no air in contact, no calcium carbonate forms and the solution stays colourless.

questions.topic: Testing Air: Lime Water and Dust
questions.question: In Activity 8.2, a clean black sheet is left near an open window for a few hours. What is observed and what does it show?
options: It fades in colour, showing oxygen in the air bleaches it
It stays unchanged, showing air contains only pure gases
Tiny particles settle on it, showing dust is suspended in air
It becomes damp, showing water vapour is present in the air
questions.explanation: Tiny particles settle on the black paper, which can be examined with a magnifying glass. This shows that dust particles are suspended in the air.

questions.topic: Testing Air: Lime Water and Dust
questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed in the chapter as a major air pollutant?
options: Ozone
Carbon monoxide
Sulfur dioxide
Argon
questions.explanation: The major pollutants named are particulate matter (dust, soot) and gases like carbon monoxide, ozone, nitrogen dioxide and sulfur dioxide. Argon is a normal component of air.

questions.topic: Testing Air: Lime Water and Dust
questions.question: Calcium oxide reacting with water releases heat.
questions.explanation: Calcium oxide reacts vigorously with water to form calcium hydroxide and releases heat.

questions.topic: Testing Air: Lime Water and Dust
questions.question: The number of dust particles in the air is the same at all places and at all times.
questions.explanation: The nature and number of dust particles vary from time to time and from place to place.

questions.question: According to Table 8.1, aerated water (soda water) is an example of which type of mixture?
options: Gas and liquid
Liquid and liquid
Solid and liquid
Gas and gas
questions.explanation: Aerated water has carbon dioxide gas dissolved in liquid water, so it is a gas-and-liquid mixture.

questions.question: Carbon particles in air form which type of mixture?
options: Solid and liquid
Solid and gas
Gas and gas
Solid and solid
questions.explanation: Carbon (soot) particles are solids suspended in air, a gas, so Table 8.1 classifies this as a solid-and-gas mixture.

questions.question: Vinegar is listed in Table 8.1 as a mixture of…
options: carbon dioxide in water (gas and liquid)
acetic acid in air (liquid and gas)
acetic acid in water (liquid and liquid)
tartaric acid in water (solid and liquid)
questions.explanation: Vinegar is acetic acid in water, a liquid-and-liquid mixture. Tartaric acid appears in baking powder; carbon dioxide in water is soda water.

questions.question: Baking powder is given as a solid–solid mixture of…
options: baking soda and common salt
baking soda and acetic acid
tartaric acid and sugar
baking soda and tartaric acid
questions.explanation: Table 8.1 lists baking powder as baking soda and tartaric acid, both solids.

questions.question: Seawater and sand-in-water belong to the same mixture type in Table 8.1 but differ in uniformity. Which is correct?
options: Both are solid–liquid; seawater is uniform, sand in water is non-uniform
Both are liquid–liquid; seawater is non-uniform, sand in water is uniform
Both are solid–liquid; both are uniform because both contain water
Both are solid–solid; sand in water is uniform, seawater is non-uniform
questions.explanation: Both are solid-and-liquid mixtures. Dissolved salt in seawater cannot be seen (uniform), whereas sand grains in water are visible (non-uniform).

questions.question: Which mixture–type pairing from Table 8.1 is WRONG?
options: Oil and water — liquid and liquid
Seawater — liquid and liquid
Air — gas and gas
Alloys — solid and solid
questions.explanation: Seawater (salt dissolved in water) is a solid-and-liquid mixture. The other three pairings match Table 8.1.

questions.question: In science, what is the purpose of separating the components of a mixture?
options: To make the mixture uniform in nature
To make the components react with each other
To obtain pure substances from the mixture
To obtain the useful component and discard the rest
questions.explanation: In everyday life we separate to get the component of interest and discard the rest; in science the purpose is to obtain pure substances.

questions.question: Which pair below contains one uniform and one non-uniform mixture?
options: Air and seawater
Sand-in-water and oil-in-water
Alloys and vinegar
Vinegar and oil-in-water
questions.explanation: Vinegar (acetic acid in water) is uniform while oil and water separate visibly (non-uniform). Air and seawater are both uniform; sand-in-water and oil-in-water are both non-uniform; alloys and vinegar are both uniform.

questions.question: In everyday life, mixtures are usually separated in order to obtain pure substances.
questions.explanation: In everyday life separation is done to obtain the component of interest and discard the others; obtaining pure substances is the purpose in science.

questions.question: Soda water is a mixture of a gas and a liquid.
questions.explanation: Aerated (soda) water is listed as a gas-and-liquid mixture in Table 8.1.

questions.question: Which of the following are solid–liquid mixtures according to Table 8.1?
options: Sand and water
Seawater
Vinegar
Soda water
questions.explanation: Sand and water and seawater are solid-and-liquid mixtures. Vinegar is liquid-liquid and soda water is gas-liquid.

questions.question: In science, a pure substance is one that…
options: has no other substance present in it
is sold without any adulteration
is made of two or more elements
cannot be seen with a microscope
questions.explanation: In science a pure substance has no other substance in it and consists of the same type of particles. 'Unadulterated' is the common-usage meaning.

questions.question: What is adulteration?
options: Heating a compound so that it breaks into its elements
Illegally adding cheaper or poor-quality substances to a product
Legally mixing two pure substances to form a uniform mixture
Separating a mixture to recover the component of interest
questions.explanation: Adulteration is the illegal process of adding substances that are cheaper or of poor quality to a product, usually to increase quantity or reduce cost.

questions.question: Why is adulteration usually carried out, according to the chapter?
options: To make the product last longer on the shelf
To make the product a pure substance
To increase quantity or reduce manufacturing cost
To improve the taste and colour of the product
questions.explanation: Adulteration is done to increase the quantity or reduce the manufacturing cost; it deteriorates quality and can be hazardous to health.

questions.question: A packet of milk is labelled 'pure'. How would a scientist classify this milk?
options: Pure, because the label says it has not been adulterated
Pure, because its particles cannot be seen separately
An element, because it cannot be separated by filtering
Impure, because it is made of more than one substance
questions.explanation: For a scientist, products that look pure are impure (mixtures) if they consist of more than one substance. Labels and invisibility of particles do not make something a pure substance.

questions.question: A pure substance cannot be separated into other kinds of matter by…
options: any physical process
any chemical process
heating alone
filtering alone
questions.explanation: A pure substance is matter that cannot be separated into other kinds of matter by any physical process. Compounds, which are pure substances, can still be broken down chemically.

questions.question: Substance X can be separated into two different substances by filtration. Based on the chapter, X must be…
options: a pure substance
a mixture
a compound
an element
questions.explanation: Only mixtures can be separated by physical processes like filtration. A pure substance (element or compound) cannot be separated into other kinds of matter physically.

questions.question: Which statement about pure substances is NOT correct?
options: A pure substance can be either an element or a compound
A pure substance cannot be separated physically into other matter
A pure substance always consists of a single element
A pure substance consists of the same type of particles
questions.explanation: Compounds like water and sugar are also pure substances, so a pure substance need not be a single element. The other statements are from the chapter.

questions.question: In science, a product labelled 'pure' is always a pure substance.
questions.explanation: Products that look pure are considered impure by scientists if they are made of more than one substance.

questions.question: A pure substance consists of only one type of particle.
questions.explanation: When a scientist says something is pure, the substance consists of the same type of particles.

questions.question: Which of the following would a scientist classify as pure substances?
options: Baking soda
Sugar
Milk
Soil
questions.explanation: Baking soda and sugar are compounds, hence pure substances. Milk and soil are made of several substances and are mixtures.

questions.question: In Activity 8.3, a few drops of which liquid were added to the water in the beaker?
options: Dilute hydrochloric acid
Lime water (calcium hydroxide)
Vinegar (acetic acid)
Dilute sulfuric acid
questions.explanation: A few drops of dilute sulfuric acid were added to the water before passing electricity. Dilute hydrochloric acid is used in Activity 8.5.

questions.question: The gas that gives a 'pop' sound when a burning candle is brought near it is…
options: hydrogen
oxygen
carbon dioxide
water vapour
questions.explanation: A pop sound indicates hydrogen gas. Oxygen makes the candle flame glow brighter.

questions.question: In which gas does the flame of a burning candle glow brighter?
options: Hydrogen sulfide
Oxygen
Hydrogen
Nitrogen
questions.explanation: Oxygen supports combustion, so a candle flame glows brighter in it; hydrogen burns with a pop.

questions.question: Why can the gases collected in Activity 8.3 NOT be water vapour?
options: Water vapour is heavier than water and would sink to the bottom
Water vapour would have turned the lime water in the beaker milky
Water vapour would have condensed back into liquid water in the tubes
Water vapour cannot form bubbles inside water-filled test tubes
questions.explanation: The chapter reasons that if the gases were water vapour they would have condensed back to form water; since they stayed as gases, they are new substances.

questions.question: What can be inferred from Activity 8.3?
options: Water is an element that cannot be broken down
Water is a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen gases
Water contains dissolved carbon dioxide
Water is composed of hydrogen and oxygen
questions.explanation: Passing electricity through water gave hydrogen and oxygen, so water is composed of these two constituents chemically combined — a compound, not a mixture or element.

questions.question: Cooling water to ice or boiling it to vapour does not change its particles, but passing electricity breaks it into hydrogen and oxygen. Which pair of labels fits?
options: Physical changes; chemical change
Chemical changes; physical change
Physical changes; physical change
Chemical changes; chemical change
questions.explanation: During freezing and boiling the particles of water remain the same (physical change). Electricity produces new substances, hydrogen and oxygen, so that is a chemical change.

questions.question: In Activity 8.3 the two test tubes collected unequal volumes of gas. Which fact from the chapter is this consistent with?
options: One terminal of the battery gives more current than the other
Water has hydrogen and oxygen atoms in a 2:1 ratio
Water has hydrogen and oxygen atoms in a 1:1 ratio
Oxygen dissolves in water more than hydrogen does
questions.explanation: The chapter states the ratio of hydrogen to oxygen atoms in water is 2:1, so more hydrogen is produced than oxygen — the gas volumes are not the same.

questions.question: Which statement about Activity 8.3 is NOT correct?
options: The activity should be done under a teacher's supervision
The test tubes were filled completely with water from the beaker
The gases collected in the test tubes were water vapour
Gas bubbles formed at both terminals of the battery
questions.explanation: The gases were hydrogen and oxygen; water vapour would have condensed back to water. The other statements are part of the procedure.

questions.question: Predict: the activity is stopped after one minute instead of 10–15 minutes. What would most likely be seen?
options: Equal volumes of gas collected in both test tubes
The water in both tubes turning milky
Both gases giving a pop sound with a candle
Only a small volume of gas collected in each tube
questions.explanation: Gas collects gradually over 10–15 minutes, so stopping early leaves only a little gas. The volumes are unequal regardless of time, lime water is not involved, and only hydrogen pops.

questions.question: A burning candle brought near oxygen gas produces a pop sound.
questions.explanation: Oxygen makes the flame glow brighter; the pop sound is the test for hydrogen.

questions.question: The beaker in Activity 8.3 was filled about two-thirds with water.
questions.explanation: The procedure says to fill 2/3rd of the beaker with water and add a few drops of dilute sulfuric acid.

questions.question: Which observations belong to Activity 8.3 (passing electricity through water)?
options: Gas bubbles at both terminals
A pop sound from one test tube
Lime water turning milky
A black mass forming
questions.explanation: Bubbles at both terminals and a pop from the hydrogen tube are from Activity 8.3. Milky lime water is Activity 8.1; the black mass is Activity 8.5.

questions.question: Each element is made up of identical particles called…
options: atoms
components
compounds
minerals
questions.explanation: Each element is made of identical particles called atoms, which differ from the atoms of any other element.

questions.question: Elements are described as the building blocks of all matter because they…
options: always exist as single atoms that never combine
cannot be broken down into simpler substances
can be separated into other substances physically
are always found as uniform mixtures in nature
questions.explanation: Elements cannot be further broken down into simpler substances, so they are the building blocks of all matter. Most atoms combine to form molecules rather than existing alone.

questions.question: A molecule of hydrogen is formed when…
options: two atoms of oxygen combine
a hydrogen atom joins an oxygen atom
two atoms of hydrogen combine
one atom of hydrogen stands alone
questions.explanation: Two atoms of hydrogen combine to form one molecule of hydrogen; similarly two oxygen atoms form an oxygen molecule.

questions.question: Why do atoms of most elements form molecules?
options: Their atoms are too heavy to move about on their own
Their atoms must join atoms of other elements to stay stable
Their atoms are visible only when joined into larger groups
Their atoms cannot exist independently, so they combine into stable particles
questions.explanation: The atoms of most elements cannot exist independently; two or more combine to form a stable particle called a molecule, such as H2 or O2 (same element).

questions.question: How many elements are known at present, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter states the number of known elements is 118, most of which are solids.

questions.question: How many elements exist as gases at room temperature, and what type are they?
options: Two, one metal and one non-metal
Eleven, all non-metals
Two, both metals
Eleven, all metals
questions.explanation: Eleven elements are gaseous at room temperature and all are non-metals (oxygen, helium, nitrogen, etc.). 'Two, one metal and one non-metal' describes the liquid elements.

questions.question: Gallium and caesium are solids, yet they turn into liquids at around…
questions.explanation: Gallium and caesium become liquid at a temperature around 30 °C (303 K), which is close to a warm room or hand temperature.

questions.question: Which statement about the states of elements is NOT correct?
options: Mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature
Most of the 118 known elements are solids
Helium is a non-metal that is a gas at room temperature
Bromine is a metal that is liquid at room temperature
questions.explanation: Bromine is a liquid non-metal; mercury is the liquid metal. The other statements match the chapter.

questions.question: Roughly how many different elements are used in manufacturing a mobile phone?
options: More than 45
Fewer than 10
Exactly 118
About 20
questions.explanation: More than 45 elements — such as aluminium, copper, silicon, cobalt, lithium, gold and silver — are used in a mobile phone's screen, battery and other components.

questions.question: A sample is a shiny solid at 20 °C but melts into a liquid when held in a warm hand (about 35 °C). Based on the chapter, it is most likely…
options: silicon
gallium
mercury
bromine
questions.explanation: Gallium (like caesium) is a solid that becomes liquid at around 30 °C. Mercury and bromine are already liquid at room temperature, and silicon is a metalloid with a very high melting point.

questions.question: 303 K corresponds to approximately 30 °C.
questions.explanation: The chapter gives the melting point of gallium and caesium as around 30 °C (303 K).

questions.question: All eleven elements that are gases at room temperature are metals.
questions.explanation: All eleven gaseous elements are non-metals, such as oxygen, helium and nitrogen.

questions.question: Select the non-metals from the list.
options: Sulfur
Hydrogen
Magnesium
Aluminium
questions.explanation: Sulfur and hydrogen are non-metals; magnesium and aluminium are metals.

questions.question: Which of these are metalloids according to the chapter?
options: Silicon
Boron
Carbon
Gallium
questions.explanation: Silicon and boron are named as metalloids. Carbon is a non-metal and gallium is a low-melting solid element.

questions.question: Compounds are formed when…
options: atoms of the same element join to form a stable molecule
a mixture is separated into its pure components physically
different elements combine in fixed ratios to form something entirely new
two or more substances mix while each keeps its own properties
questions.explanation: A compound forms when different elements combine chemically in fixed ratios to form an entirely new substance with different properties.

questions.question: Why can hydrogen and oxygen in water not be separated by physical means?
options: Both gases are colourless and so cannot be identified for separation
They are present in such small amounts that filtration cannot catch them
Hydrogen escapes from water as soon as any physical method is tried
Their particles are so tightly attached that physical methods cannot pull them apart
questions.explanation: In water the particles of hydrogen and oxygen are so tightly attached that it is generally impossible to separate them by physical methods — which is why water is a compound.

questions.question: The ratio of the number of hydrogen atoms to oxygen atoms in water is…
questions.explanation: Water molecules contain hydrogen and oxygen in a fixed ratio of 2:1 atoms. 1:1 is the ratio in sodium chloride; 4:1 is the copper-to-tin ratio in Kamsya.

questions.question: Sodium is a soft metal and chlorine is a hazardous gas, yet sodium chloride is harmless and taste-enhancing. What does this illustrate?
options: Compounds always have the properties of the more abundant element
A compound's properties differ from those of its constituent elements
A mixture's components retain their original properties
Elements cannot combine unless both are metals
questions.explanation: The properties of a compound are different from those of the elements forming it; sodium chloride is nothing like soft sodium or hazardous chlorine.

questions.question: In sodium chloride, particles of sodium and chlorine are present in the ratio…
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride is made of particles of sodium and chlorine in a 1:1 ratio; water's H:O ratio is 2:1.

questions.question: Dissolved common salt can be separated from water by evaporation. Can sodium chloride itself be split into sodium and chlorine by a physical process?
options: Yes — further evaporation separates the sodium from the chlorine
Yes — a magnet removes the sodium, leaving chlorine behind
No — because sodium and chlorine are both gases at room temperature
No — it is a compound whose elements are chemically combined
questions.explanation: Evaporation separates the mixture (salt + water), but sodium chloride is a compound and its constituent elements cannot be separated by any physical method. Sodium is a soft metal, not a gas.

questions.question: When sugar is heated gently in a boiling tube, it first…
options: turns brown and later chars to black
melts into a clear colourless liquid
gives off a gas with a rotten-egg smell
turns white and then evaporates
questions.explanation: On heating, sugar turns brown and then begins to char, turning blackish, leaving charcoal (carbon) behind.

questions.question: Water droplets appear near the open end of the boiling tube while heating dry sugar. Where did this water come from?
options: From moisture trapped inside the glass of the tube
From the sugar itself, because the tube was being heated
From water vapour in the air condensing on the warm tube
From the spirit lamp flame burning hydrogen gas
questions.explanation: Since the tube is being heated, water vapour from the air would not condense on it; the water must have come from the dry sugar, showing sugar contains hydrogen and oxygen.

questions.question: Why can sugar NOT be an element?
options: It is a solid that turns brown when heated gently
It tastes sweet, unlike any of the known elements
It decomposes into carbon and water, which contains hydrogen and oxygen
It dissolves completely in water to form a uniform mixture
questions.explanation: Elements cannot be broken into simpler substances. Sugar decomposes on heating into carbon and water (hydrogen + oxygen), so it is a compound of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

questions.question: 'Hydrogen is a fuel, oxygen supports combustion, whereas water extinguishes fire.' Which conclusion does this support?
options: Water is a uniform mixture of hydrogen and oxygen
Water keeps the fire-supporting property of oxygen
Hydrogen and oxygen lose their mass when they form water
A compound's properties are entirely different from its elements'
questions.explanation: Water (a compound) extinguishes fire although it is made from a fuel and a combustion supporter — the properties of a compound differ from those of its constituent elements. A mixture would have kept their properties.

questions.question: Which statement about compounds is NOT correct?
options: The elements in a compound can be separated by evaporation or filtration
Elements combine in a fixed ratio to form a compound
A compound's properties differ from those of its elements
Water and sodium chloride are examples of compounds
questions.explanation: The constituent elements of a compound cannot be separated by any physical method such as evaporation or filtration. The other statements are correct.

questions.question: In Activity 8.4, the water droplets in the boiling tube came from condensation of moisture in the air.
questions.explanation: Because the tube was being heated, the water must have come from the dry sugar itself, not from the air.

questions.question: Sugar decomposes on heating to give carbon and water.
questions.explanation: Sugar decomposes on heating into carbon (charcoal) and water, showing it is a compound of C, H and O.

questions.question: Which of the following are compounds?
options: Water
Sodium chloride
Oxygen
Bronze
questions.explanation: Water and sodium chloride are compounds. Oxygen is an element and bronze is an alloy (mixture).

questions.question: Sample A (iron filings mixed with sulfur powder) is best described as…
options: a non-uniform mixture of two compounds
a non-uniform mixture of two elements
a uniform mixture of two elements
a compound of iron and sulfur
questions.explanation: Sample A is a mixture of the elements iron and sulfur; its black and yellow particles can still be seen, so it is non-uniform.

questions.question: The black mass obtained by heating Sample A (Sample B) is…
options: a uniform mixture of iron and sulfur
charcoal left after burning sulfur
iron sulfide, a compound
iron chloride, a compound
questions.explanation: Heating iron and sulfur together forms iron sulfide, a new compound with the same colour and texture throughout.

questions.question: What happens when a magnet is moved over Sample A and Sample B?
options: Both samples are attracted equally strongly
Sample B is attracted; Sample A is not attracted
Neither sample is attracted by the magnet
Iron in Sample A is attracted; Sample B is not attracted
questions.explanation: In the mixture, iron retains its magnetic property and is attracted. In Sample B, iron has combined into iron sulfide, which is not attracted.

questions.question: Why does the magnet have no effect on Sample B?
options: Iron has combined chemically into a new substance with different properties
The heat has permanently destroyed the magnetism of the iron filings
The sulfur coats each iron particle and blocks the magnetic pull
Grinding in the mortar broke the iron into pieces too small to attract
questions.explanation: Sample B is iron sulfide, a compound whose properties are completely different from iron and sulfur; the iron no longer exists as free iron, so it is not attracted.

questions.question: When dilute hydrochloric acid is added to Sample A, which gas is evolved?
options: Carbon dioxide
Hydrogen
Hydrogen sulfide
Oxygen
questions.explanation: Iron in the mixture reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form iron chloride and hydrogen gas — colourless, odourless, burns with a pop.

questions.question: When dilute hydrochloric acid is added to Sample B (iron sulfide), the gas evolved…
options: is oxygen that makes a candle glow brighter
is carbon dioxide that turns lime water milky
is hydrogen sulfide with a rotten-egg odour
is hydrogen that burns with a pop sound
questions.explanation: Iron sulfide + dilute hydrochloric acid → iron chloride + hydrogen sulfide; the gas is colourless with a rotten egg-like smell.

questions.question: After the acid reaction with Sample A, a yellow solid remains at the bottom of the test tube. What does this show?
options: Iron has not reacted with the acid
Iron sulfide has formed in the test tube
The acid was too dilute to react with anything
Sulfur does not react with hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: The yellow solid is sulfur, left behind because sulfur does not react with hydrochloric acid, while the iron reacted to give hydrogen.

questions.question: Which statement about Activity 8.5 is NOT correct?
options: Sample B can be separated into iron and sulfur using a magnet
Sample A shows black and yellow particles side by side
Sample B has the same colour and texture throughout
Both samples give off a gas with dilute hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: Sample B is iron sulfide, a compound; iron and sulfur can no longer be separated and it is not attracted by a magnet. The other statements are correct observations.

questions.question: What is the single change made to turn Sample A into Sample B?
options: Dissolving the mixture in water and filtering
Heating the mixture until a black mass forms
Adding dilute hydrochloric acid to the mixture
Passing a magnet over the mixture repeatedly
questions.explanation: Half of Sample A is heated in a china dish with stirring until a black mass forms; cooling and grinding give Sample B. Heating causes the elements to combine chemically.

questions.question: Which evidence from Activity 8.5 shows that a new substance was formed on heating?
options: The product can be separated back into iron and sulfur by a magnet
The product still shows black and yellow particles side by side
The product is uniform, not magnetic, and gives a different gas with acid
The product weighs less than the mixture and is yellow in colour
questions.explanation: Iron sulfide has completely different properties: uniform colour and texture, no magnetic attraction, and hydrogen sulfide (rotten-egg smell) instead of hydrogen with acid.

questions.question: A student heats half of Sample A for only a short time, so no black mass forms. Predict the magnet test on this heated portion.
options: Nothing is attracted, since heating always removes magnetism
Only the sulfur is attracted, since it melted onto the iron
The whole mass is attracted as a single lump of iron sulfide
Iron filings are still attracted, since no compound has formed
questions.explanation: Without the chemical change, iron and sulfur remain a mixture and iron keeps its properties, so the magnet still attracts it. Only iron sulfide (the black mass) is non-magnetic.

questions.question: Sample B (iron sulfide) is attracted by a magnet.
questions.explanation: Iron sulfide is a compound with different properties from iron; it is not attracted by a magnet.

questions.question: Hydrogen sulfide gas has an odour like rotten eggs.
questions.explanation: The gas from iron sulfide and dilute hydrochloric acid is colourless with a rotten egg-like odour.

questions.question: Sulfur reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to give hydrogen gas.
questions.explanation: Sulfur does not react with hydrochloric acid and is left as a yellow solid; it is iron that gives hydrogen.

questions.question: Which are properties of the gas evolved when Sample A reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid?
options: Colourless
Burns with a 'pop' sound
Smells of rotten eggs
Makes a candle glow brighter
questions.explanation: The gas is hydrogen: colourless, odourless, and burns with a pop. Rotten-egg smell is hydrogen sulfide (Sample B) and a brighter flame indicates oxygen.

questions.question: Which substances used in Activity 8.5 are elements?
options: Iron
Sulfur
Iron sulfide
Hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: Iron and sulfur are elements; iron sulfide is a compound and hydrochloric acid is a compound in solution.

questions.topic: Uses of Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
questions.question: Elements like iron and aluminium are used to construct…
options: bridges, buildings and vehicles
medicines, vaccines and fertilisers
talcum powder and cement
beeswax moulds for Dhokra art
questions.explanation: Iron and aluminium are used to build bridges, buildings and vehicles; medicines and fertilisers come from chemists' knowledge of compounds.

questions.topic: Uses of Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
questions.question: How does understanding how elements combine help chemists, according to the chapter?
options: They can measure the air quality index of a city
They can invent life-saving medicines, vaccines and fertilisers
They can turn mixtures back into pure elements by heating
They can make elements that are lighter than graphene aerogel
questions.explanation: Chemists study how elements combine to create compounds, enabling medicines and vaccines, and the creation of fertilisers to enhance crop production.

questions.topic: Uses of Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
questions.question: Wood, steel and concrete used as building materials are all…
options: elements
minerals
mixtures
compounds
questions.explanation: The chapter states that wood, steel and concrete are all mixtures.

questions.topic: Uses of Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
questions.question: Graphene aerogel is said to be the lightest material on Earth and is made from…
options: aluminium
silicon
hydrogen
carbon
questions.explanation: Graphene aerogel is made from carbon and is so light that grass can hold it.

questions.topic: Uses of Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
questions.question: Why can graphene aerogel potentially be used to clean up oil spills?
options: It is highly porous and so has a high absorbing capacity
It reacts chemically with oil to form harmless water
It is heavy enough to sink and trap oil on the seabed
It dissolves oil because it is made of liquid carbon
questions.explanation: Graphene aerogel is highly porous and therefore has a high absorbing capacity, which is why it could act as an environmental cleaner for oil spills on sea and land.

questions.topic: Uses of Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
questions.question: Which statement about materials is NOT correct?
options: Graphene aerogel is light enough for grass to hold it
Graphene aerogel is a compound of carbon and oxygen
Stainless steel is stronger and more durable than pure iron
Steel and concrete are mixtures used as building materials
questions.explanation: Graphene aerogel is made from carbon alone (an element), not a carbon–oxygen compound. The other statements appear in the chapter.

questions.topic: Uses of Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
questions.question: Why did engineers and material scientists develop stainless steel?
options: To make a compound of iron and carbon in a fixed ratio
To make the lightest known material for cleaning oil spills
To obtain a material stronger and more durable than pure iron
To obtain a pure element that does not rust in moist air
questions.explanation: Material scientists design mixtures with unique properties; stainless steel is an alloy that is stronger and more durable than pure iron.

questions.topic: Uses of Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
questions.question: Graphene aerogel is so heavy that grass cannot hold it.
questions.explanation: Graphene aerogel is said to be the lightest material on Earth — so light that even grass can hold it.

questions.topic: Uses of Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
questions.question: Knowledge of how elements combine has helped in creating fertilisers that increase crop production.
questions.explanation: The chapter says this knowledge helps create fertilisers, enhancing crop production for a growing population.

questions.question: Most rocks are described in the chapter as…
options: a single pure compound
a native element
a uniform alloy
a mixture of minerals
questions.explanation: Most rocks are a mixture of minerals that can be seen with the eyes, a magnifying glass or a microscope.

questions.question: What are native minerals?
options: Minerals that are pure elements, not compounds
Minerals that are mixtures of several compounds
Minerals found only in Indian rocks
Minerals that contain water in a fixed ratio
questions.explanation: Native minerals are pure elements such as gold, silver, copper (metals) or sulfur and carbon (non-metals).

questions.question: Most minerals are…
options: non-uniform mixtures of rocks
compounds made up of more than one element
pure elements found uncombined
uniform mixtures of several metals
questions.explanation: Most minerals are compounds of more than one element; only some (native minerals) are pure elements, and minerals are never mixtures.

questions.question: Cement is made from…
options: iron, nickel, chromium and carbon
copper, tin, calcite and sand
calcite, quartz, alumina and iron oxide
talc, mica, olivine and pyroxene
questions.explanation: Cement is made from calcite, quartz, alumina and iron oxide, which are minerals or obtained from minerals.

questions.question: Talcum powder is made from the mineral…
options: mica
calcite
quartz
talc
questions.explanation: Talcum powder is made from the mineral talc.

questions.question: According to the Snapshots, minerals are…
options: natural solid substances with a fixed chemical composition
man-made solid mixtures with a variable composition
natural liquids or gases trapped inside rocks
natural substances that are always pure elements
questions.explanation: Minerals are natural, solid substances found on Earth with a fixed chemical composition; most are compounds and rarely pure elements.

questions.question: Which statement about minerals is NOT correct?
options: Most rocks are mixtures of minerals
All minerals are compounds of two or more elements
Some minerals are pure elements such as gold and sulfur
Minerals have a fixed chemical composition
questions.explanation: Most, but not all, minerals are compounds; native minerals like gold, silver, copper, sulfur and carbon are pure elements.

questions.question: How can gold be classified as both a mineral and a metal? (Exercise Q12)
options: It is a mixture of several metals found naturally in rocks
It is a metal that becomes a mineral only after it is refined
It is a native mineral found as a pure element, and that element is a metal
It is a compound mineral that contains a metal in a fixed ratio
questions.explanation: Gold occurs naturally as a native mineral — a mineral that is a pure element rather than a compound — and as an element it is a metal.

questions.question: Talc is one of the minerals used to make cement.
questions.explanation: Cement is made from calcite, quartz, alumina and iron oxide; talc is used for talcum powder.

questions.question: Copper can occur as a native mineral.
questions.explanation: Native minerals are pure elements and include metals such as gold, silver and copper.

questions.question: Which native minerals named in the chapter are non-metals?
options: Sulfur
Carbon
Gold
Copper
questions.explanation: Native minerals can be metals (gold, silver, copper) or non-metals (sulfur, carbon).

questions.question: Matter is defined in the chapter as anything that…
options: can be seen with the naked eye
is made of two or more elements
can be melted by heating
has mass and takes up space
questions.explanation: Matter is everything that has mass and takes up space; elements and compounds are its building blocks.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT made of matter, according to the chapter?
options: Thoughts
Dust
Water vapour
Charcoal
questions.explanation: Thoughts and emotions, like light, heat and electricity, are not made of matter. Dust, water vapour and charcoal are matter.

questions.question: Dhokra art is an old craft from which states?
options: Punjab and Haryana
Bihar and Odisha
Kerala and Tamil Nadu
Gujarat and Rajasthan
questions.explanation: Dhokra art is an old craft from Bihar and Odisha that uses metals to create figures inspired by nature.

questions.question: What is the first step in making a Dhokra figure?
options: Melting bronze in a clay furnace
Carving the figure from hardened clay
Shaping the design in beeswax
Covering a clay core with molten brass
questions.explanation: The process begins by shaping a design in beeswax; the wax model is then covered with clay to make a mould.

questions.question: In Dhokra art, after the clay mould hardens, what happens next?
options: The clay is broken away to reveal the finished wax figure
Molten metal is poured over the outside of the clay mould
The mould is filled with more beeswax to strengthen it
The wax is melted out, leaving a hollow space for molten metal
questions.explanation: Once the clay hardens, the wax is melted out, leaving a hollow space that is filled with molten brass or bronze.

questions.question: Which metal mixtures give Dhokra art its strength and shiny golden colour?
options: Brass or bronze
Iron or steel
Gold or silver
Copper or tin
questions.explanation: The hollow mould is filled with molten brass or bronze, which makes Dhokra art strong and gives it a shiny golden colour.

questions.question: Which option lists the Dhokra steps in the correct order?
options: Wax model → pour molten metal → clay cover → melt out wax
Wax model → clay cover → melt out wax → pour molten metal
Clay cover → wax model → pour molten metal → melt out wax
Pour molten metal → wax model → clay cover → melt out wax
questions.explanation: The design is shaped in beeswax, covered with clay, the wax is melted out after the clay hardens, and the hollow is filled with molten brass or bronze.

questions.question: Electricity is a form of matter.
questions.explanation: Light, heat, electricity, thoughts and emotions are not made of matter.

questions.question: In Dhokra art the clay mould is made first and then filled with beeswax.
questions.explanation: The beeswax model is made first; clay is applied over it to form the mould, and the wax is later melted out.

questions.question: A + B → C, where A and B cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical reactions. Which statement is correct?
options: C is a compound, and A and B have no fixed composition
A and B are compounds, and C has a fixed composition
A and B are elements; C is a compound and has a fixed composition
A, B and C are all compounds and only C has a fixed composition
questions.explanation: Substances that cannot be broken down further are elements, so A and B are elements. Their product C, formed from two elements, is a compound with a fixed composition.

questions.question: Assertion: Air is a mixture. Reason: A mixture is formed when two or more substances are mixed without undergoing any chemical change. Choose the correct option.
options: Both are true but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
The Assertion is true but the Reason is false
The Assertion is false but the Reason is true
Both are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
questions.explanation: Air's gases are mixed without chemical change, which is exactly why air is a mixture — so both statements are true and the Reason explains the Assertion.

questions.question: Water has properties different from hydrogen and oxygen because…
options: the elements are chemically combined in a fixed ratio to form a new substance
the elements are merely mixed and each keeps its own properties
water contains more oxygen than hydrogen by number of atoms
hydrogen and oxygen lose their mass when they turn into water
questions.explanation: Water is a compound: hydrogen and oxygen combine chemically in a 2:1 ratio to form an entirely new substance, so its properties differ from those of its elements.

questions.question: In which option are ALL the examples correctly matched?
options: Non-uniform mixtures — air, sand, brass, muddy water
Pure substances — carbon dioxide, iron, oxygen, sugar
Elements — water, nitrogen, iron, air
Uniform mixtures — minerals, seawater, bronze, air
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide and sugar are compounds and iron and oxygen are elements — all pure substances. Water is a compound and air a mixture (not elements); minerals are mostly compounds; air and brass are uniform mixtures.

questions.question: Why is 'Elements — water, nitrogen, iron, air' an incorrect match?
options: Water is a mixture and nitrogen is a compound
Iron is a compound and air is an element
Water is a compound and air is a mixture
Nitrogen is a compound and iron is a mixture
questions.explanation: Only nitrogen and iron are elements in that list; water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen, and air is a mixture of gases.

questions.question: Why is 'Non-uniform mixtures — air, sand, brass, muddy water' an incorrect match?
options: Sand and muddy water are compounds
Brass is an element and air is a compound
Muddy water is a uniform mixture
Air and brass are uniform mixtures
questions.explanation: Air and brass (an alloy) are uniform mixtures whose components cannot be seen separately. Sand and muddy water are indeed non-uniform mixtures.

questions.question: Iron reacts with moist air to form iron oxide. Classify iron, moist air and iron oxide respectively.
options: Element, mixture, compound
Compound, mixture, element
Element, compound, mixture
Mixture, element, compound
questions.explanation: Iron is an element, moist air is a mixture of gases and water vapour, and iron oxide is a compound of iron and oxygen.

questions.question: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Which classification is correct?
options: Magnesium is a mixture; oxygen is an element; magnesium oxide is a compound
Magnesium and oxygen are elements; magnesium oxide is a compound
Magnesium is an element; oxygen and magnesium oxide are mixtures
Magnesium and oxygen are compounds; magnesium oxide is an element
questions.explanation: Magnesium and oxygen are elements; they combine chemically in a fixed ratio to form the compound magnesium oxide.

questions.question: From the reactions in Exercise Q5, select the compounds.
options: Iron oxide
Magnesium oxide
Moist air
Magnesium
questions.explanation: Iron oxide and magnesium oxide are compounds formed from two elements. Moist air is a mixture and magnesium is an element.

questions.question: From Exercise Q6, select the elements.
options: Aluminium
Nitrogen
Rust
Glucose
Seawater
questions.explanation: Aluminium and nitrogen are elements. Rust (iron oxide) and glucose are compounds; seawater is a mixture.

questions.question: From Exercise Q6, select the mixtures.
options: Muddy water
Fruit juice
Baking soda
Iron sulfide
questions.explanation: Muddy water and fruit juice are mixtures of several substances. Baking soda and iron sulfide are compounds.

questions.question: From Exercise Q6, select the compounds.
options: Sodium chloride
Magnesium oxide
Sulfur
Sand
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride and magnesium oxide are compounds. Sulfur is an element and sand is a mixture.

questions.question: From the Exercise Q6 list, which of these is a pure substance?
options: Air
Fruit juice
Glucose
Sand
questions.explanation: Glucose is a compound, hence a pure substance. Sand, air and fruit juice are mixtures.

questions.question: Which of these from Exercise Q6 is NOT a pure substance?
options: Rust
Gold
Carbon dioxide
Seawater
questions.explanation: Seawater is a mixture of salts and water. Rust and carbon dioxide are compounds and gold is an element — all pure substances.

questions.question: When a mixture of iron filings and sulfur powder is heated, which new substance forms and how does it differ from the mixture?
options: Iron sulfide; it is non-magnetic and cannot be separated into iron and sulfur
Iron chloride; it is magnetic and can be separated by a magnet
Iron oxide; it is yellow and reacts with acid to give oxygen
Iron sulfide; it still shows separate black and yellow particles
questions.explanation: Heating forms the compound iron sulfide: Iron + Sulfur → Iron sulfide. Unlike the mixture it is uniform, not attracted by a magnet, and its elements cannot be separated.

questions.question: Can a substance be classified as both an element and a compound?
options: No — because every compound is really a mixture of elements, not a single substance
No — an element cannot be broken down; a compound is made of two or more elements
Yes — any substance with a fixed composition can be called either an element or a compound
Yes — native minerals such as gold are both an element and a compound at the same time
questions.explanation: The definitions exclude each other: an element cannot be broken into simpler substances, whereas a compound is formed from two or more elements chemically combined.

questions.question: If water were a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen instead of a compound, which would be true?
options: 'Water' would extinguish fire even more effectively than it does now
Hydrogen and oxygen could not be separated from it by any physical method
Hydrogen and oxygen would keep their properties, so 'water' would support burning
Hydrogen and oxygen would still be in a fixed 2:1 ratio by atoms
questions.explanation: In a mixture each component retains its properties: hydrogen (a fuel) and oxygen (supports combustion) would make it a fire hazard, could be separated physically, and would have no fixed ratio.

questions.question: In Fig. 8.24, iron filings are placed in dilute hydrochloric acid and Gas A is collected. Identify Gas A.
options: Hydrogen sulfide
Oxygen
Chlorine
Hydrogen
questions.explanation: Iron + Dilute hydrochloric acid → Iron chloride + Hydrogen. Hydrogen sulfide forms only from iron sulfide.

questions.question: Which compound is made only from non-metals?
options: Water
Sodium chloride
Iron sulfide
Magnesium oxide
questions.explanation: Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen, both non-metals. Sodium chloride, iron sulfide and magnesium oxide each contain a metal.

questions.question: Select the compounds made only from non-metals.
options: Carbon dioxide
Sugar
Iron oxide
Sodium chloride
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide (C, O) and sugar (C, H, O) contain only non-metals. Iron oxide and sodium chloride contain the metals iron and sodium.

questions.question: In Exercise Q1, since A and B cannot be broken down chemically, they must be compounds.
questions.explanation: Substances that cannot be broken down into simpler substances are elements, not compounds.

questions.question: Rust (iron oxide) is a compound, not a mixture.
questions.explanation: Rust is iron oxide, formed when iron combines chemically with oxygen from moist air; it is a compound.
